Demand is variable and often high: observed daily sales were 0–8 units, with 8 occurring four times. Recent sequence: 8, 3, 4, 8, 1, 3, 8, 0, 5. Stockouts occurred repeatedly when available inventory and inbound supply were insufficient, and stockout penalties (2–6 per day) greatly exceeded the 0.50 ordering cost. Holding cost is low (roughly 0.10–1.00/day).

Lead time appears to be up to two days; review “arriving over the next 2 days” before ordering. Orders placed today can prevent future shortages, but do not assume same-day availability. Keep enough inventory/inbound coverage for approximately 4–5 units/day, with extra buffer for an 8-unit day. When on-hand is near zero and receipts are not enough, order at least 5–8 units rather than waiting. Avoid zero orders during consecutive stockout risk.

Examples:
- Day 5: ordering 8 was preferable to allowing a 6.00 stockout penalty.
- Days 6–9: repeated stockouts show that small or zero orders were inadequate despite inbound shipments.
- Day 10: ordering 5 alongside a 5-unit near-term receipt avoided stockout at low cost.

Operational notes (forklift certification, receiving temp, pickup time, cycle count) have not demonstrated a direct demand effect. They may affect receipt reliability, so maintain a larger buffer when fulfillment could be disrupted. Reconcile inventory counts when operational events or cycle counts occur.

Demand is variable and has increased: recent sales range 0–11 units, with several high days (8, 10, 11) and average roughly 4–5/day. Stockouts are costly (typically 1–8/day) versus the 0.50 ordering cost; holding cost is usually low (about 0.10–1.00/day).

Lead time is up to two days, and today’s order may not be available immediately. Review on-hand plus arrivals for both upcoming days before ordering. Maintain coverage for at least 4–5/day, with a substantial buffer for 8–11-unit demand. When on-hand is zero or low and near-term receipts do not cover demand, order 5–8 units or more; do not wait for receipts if projected coverage is marginal. Consecutive stockout risk warrants larger orders.

Recent evidence:
- Day 11: on-hand 1 plus only 5 arriving; ordering 8 still incurred an 8-unit stockout, confirming orders cannot reliably prevent same-day shortages.
- Days 12–13: orders of 5 were adequate when receipts were already 8/5 and stockout exposure was low.
- Day 14: ordering 0 with 5 on hand and 5/5 inbound led to a 2-unit stockout; keep some replenishment even when receipts look adequate.
- Day 15: ordering 8 avoided stockout after a 10-unit day.
- Day 16: ordering 8 was insufficient against an 8-unit stockout when no immediate receipt arrived; protect the first day of the lead time.
- Days 17–19: orders of 5 maintained service with strong inbound coverage.
- Day 20: ordering 8 still incurred a 3-unit stockout after a 7-unit day, so increase the buffer when starting at zero.

Operational notes (receiving temps, pickup timing, forklift certification, cycle counts) show no direct demand effect, but may reduce receipt reliability; use extra buffer and reconcile counts after operational events.

Demand is variable but elevated: recent sales range 0–11 units, averaging about 5–6/day, with frequent 7–9-unit days and occasional 10–11 peaks. Stockouts are far more costly than ordering (typically 1–8/day versus 0.50); holding cost is modest but accumulates when inventory is high.

Lead time is up to two days, and today’s order may not arrive immediately. Evaluate on-hand plus each of the next two days’ receipts against expected demand. Protect the first lead-time day especially when on-hand is zero: orders cannot reliably prevent same-day shortages. Starting at zero with weak/no immediate receipt, order roughly 8–10+; consecutive stockout risk justifies the high end.

With receipts already around 8/5 or 8/8 and on-hand near 1–6, orders of 5 generally maintained service (Days 12–13, 17–19, 23, 27–28), while 8 also protected service but increased holding. Recent orders of 8 on Days 24–26 and 10 on Day 22 avoided stockouts, though inventory and holding costs rose. Do not over-order when on-hand is already 6–11 and inbound is strong; 5 is usually adequate, but avoid ordering zero after prior evidence of demand.

Day 14 showed that even 5 on hand plus 5/5 inbound could still stock out; retain a small replenishment buffer. Day 20 confirmed that starting at zero needs extra cover. Demand spikes (7–11) remain plausible, so maintain roughly 4–5/day baseline coverage plus buffer when receipts are uncertain.

Receiving temps, pickup changes, forklift/racking work, and cycle counts have no demonstrated demand effect, but may impair receipt/count reliability. Add modest buffer during such events and reconcile inventory afterward.

Demand is variable but recently moderate: latest sales are mostly 3–5 units/day, while the broader history averages about 5–6/day and includes frequent 7–9-unit days and occasional 10–11 peaks. Stockouts are far costlier than ordering (typically 1–8/day versus 0.50), but holding cost becomes significant at elevated inventory.

Lead time is up to two days, and today’s order may not arrive immediately. Evaluate on-hand plus each of the next two days’ receipts against expected demand. Protect the first lead-time day, especially from zero; orders cannot reliably prevent same-day shortages. Starting at zero with weak/no immediate receipt, order roughly 8–10+.

When on-hand is 8–13 and inbound is around 5/5, repeated orders of 5 maintained service but left inventory high (Days 31–40, no stockouts). With this much cover and recent 3–5 demand, 0–3 may be appropriate; avoid automatic 5s when holding cost dominates. Day 38’s 0 order was safe with 12 on hand and 3/5 inbound. A 5 order remains prudent when on-hand approaches 6 or receipts are uncertain/missing. Do not order zero after a sharp demand spike or when projected two-day cover is thin.

Day 14 showed that 5 on hand plus 5/5 inbound can still stock out; retain a small buffer. Day 20 confirmed that zero starting inventory needs extra cover. Maintain roughly 4–5/day baseline coverage plus buffer when demand or receipts are uncertain.

Carrier pickup changes, receiving temps, forklift/racking work, and cycle counts showed no demonstrated demand effect. They may impair receipt/count reliability, so add a modest buffer only when cover is tight and reconcile inventory afterward.

Demand remains variable: typical sales are 3–5/day, with frequent 7–9 days and occasional 10+ spikes. Recent 14-day history still supports planning around 5–6/day, with a meaningful surge risk. Stockouts cost far more than ordering (roughly 1–8/day versus 0.50), but excess inventory incurs substantial holding cost.

Lead time is up to two days, and today’s order may not arrive immediately. Evaluate on-hand plus each of the next two days’ receipts against demand. Protect the first lead-time day; ordering cannot reliably prevent a same-day shortage. At zero stock with weak or delayed receipts, order roughly 8–10+, and consider 10–12 after repeated sellouts or a recent 9–10-unit spike.

Low cover needs more buffer than previously assumed: Day 42 stocked out from 2 on hand with 5/5 inbound after 9 sales; Day 49 had 4 on hand, 3/3 inbound, then a 10-unit day and still stocked out despite ordering 8. When on-hand is 0–4 and projected cover is thin, prioritize extra protection (often 8–12), though recognize same-day shortages may be unavoidable. Day 50 confirms that even ordering 10 cannot fix zero same-day stock when receipts are delayed.

When on-hand is 8–14 with reliable receipts and recent demand near 3–5, reduce orders to 0–3 or skip ordering; repeated 5s created costly excess (Days 45–48). A 5-unit order is more appropriate near 6 on hand, after a spike, or when receipts are uncertain. Do not order zero after a sharp spike or with thin two-day cover.

Operational changes, cycle counts, receiving temps, carrier timing, and racking work show no demonstrated demand effect, but may reduce receipt/count reliability; add only a modest buffer when cover is tight and reconcile afterward.

Demand has shifted higher and remains volatile: recent sales frequently run 6–10/day, with occasional 2–5 days. Plan around roughly 6–7/day while retaining meaningful 9–10+ surge risk. Stockouts cost far more than ordering (about 1–11/day versus 0.50), but excess inventory still carries holding cost.

Lead time is up to two days, and receipts may be delayed or absent on day one. Evaluate on-hand plus each of the next two days’ receipts against demand, but protect the first lead-time day: ordering cannot reliably prevent a same-day shortage. Zero stock with no same-day receipt is especially dangerous; Day 60 incurred an 11-unit stockout cost despite 12 arriving the following day. At zero stock with weak or delayed receipts, order roughly 10–12+; after a recent 8–10 sale or repeated sellouts, favor the high end.

Low cover requires substantial buffer. Recent evidence includes stockouts from 3 on hand with 5 inbound after 6 sales, and from 2 on hand with only 5 arriving first after a 10-unit day—even after ordering 12. When on-hand is 0–4 and first-day cover is thin or uncertain, generally order 8–12+, recognizing same-day shortages may still be unavoidable.

When on-hand is 8–14 with reliable receipts and demand near 3–5, reduce orders to 0–3 or skip. With on-hand near 2–6, do not automatically skip after spikes; however, strong receipts can justify zero (Day 58 had 2 on hand and [10,5] inbound with no shortage).

Carrier timing, receiving temps, and cycle counts show no demonstrated demand effect, but can reduce receipt/count reliability. Add a modest buffer when cover is tight and reconcile afterward.

Demand remains volatile, usually about 6–7/day, with frequent 8–10+ days and occasional zero/low days. Stockout costs greatly exceed ordering cost, but excess stock has meaningful holding cost.

Lead time is up to two days; day-one receipts may be zero, delayed, or insufficient. Assess on-hand plus both future receipts, but recognize today’s order cannot prevent a same-day shortage. Zero stock with strong receipts can still justify ordering about 12 (Days 61 and 65); zero stock with weak/late first receipt is especially risky. After a recent 8–12 sale or repeated sellouts, favor 10–12+.

Low on-hand (0–4) remains dangerous when first-day cover is thin: even 3 on hand with 8 inbound and demand around 6 can stock out, and 8 on hand with no day-one receipt still stocked out after a 12-unit day despite ordering 10. Use a substantial buffer, but do not expect ordering to fix immediate exposure.

Strong inbound can justify skipping: 5 on hand with [10,12] and 2 on hand with [10,12] had no shortage at zero order. With 8–10 on hand and reliable first-day receipts, 0–4 is generally enough. With 9–14 on hand and no/weak receipts, avoid automatic large orders; Day 68’s 8 order at 13 on hand incurred holding cost, while Day 69’s 3 order at 9 on hand avoided shortage.

Recent receiving temps, carrier timing, forklift work, and counts show no demonstrated demand effect, but may reduce receipt/count reliability. Add only a modest buffer when cover is tight and reconcile afterward.
